text: AI should be tracked as a physical-compute, advanced-packaging, power, cooling, networking, and grid-capacity buildout rather than only a model, software, or GPU theme.
HBM and advanced-packaging test/inspection remains the best-evidenced Layer 1 chokepoint lane, with Camtek, FormFactor, Onto, Cohu, and Kulicke & Soffa requiring deeper validation.
Data-center electrical, cooling, construction, and distributed-power names should remain in the universe as underfollowed hypotheses, but require segment-level evidence before promotion.
The merged universe needs current market-cap, valuation, analyst-count, liquidity, backlog, customer-concentration, and segment-revenue screens before Layer 2 scoring.

Non-U.S. supplier coverage is insufficient; next pass should add Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Europe, and selected A-share/HK suppliers in substrates, chemicals, probe cards, optical components, precision parts, and grid equipment.
Carry forward AI chain as a multi-bottleneck system: demand is not only accelerators, but also HBM, advanced packaging, substrates, optics, power, cooling, and grid interconnection.

ABF substrates and ABF film allocation are high-priority hidden bottleneck candidates because complexity, supplier concentration, long qualification cycles, and customer prepayments point to limited substitutability.
HBM and advanced-packaging inspection, metrology, probe cards, and known-good-die test should be treated as qualification-gated bottleneck nodes rather than generic semiconductor equipment.

High-end AI-server MLCCs are a candidate narrow bottleneck within the passive-component market; the signal to verify is AI-specific product mix, utilization, backlog, and pricing rather than aggregate MLCC demand.

Precision substrates for 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers are a low-attention optical-interconnect bottleneck candidate, especially if supplier count and qualification timing are confirmed by primary sources.

Megawatt availability, grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, and electrical balance-of-plant should be elevated in the AI funnel because physical power constraints can delay AI capacity even when chips are available.

Customer prepayments, multi-quarter supply commitments, co-funded capacity expansion, or backlog disclosures are stronger catalysts than generic AI press releases because they reveal allocation anxiety.
Technology transitions to HBM4/HBM4E, 1.6T optics, higher rack densities, and liquid cooling should be tracked as chokepoint catalysts across test, substrates, optics, power, and cooling nodes.

Need primary-source verification for substrate customer prepayments, ABF film allocation mechanics, optical precision substrate supplier count, and grid/power delay estimates before assigning company-level conviction.

For low-attention industrial names in power and cooling, verify AI-specific revenue mix, customer concentration, backlog quality, lead times, and whether growth is distinct from ordinary industrial or HVAC cyclicality.

CAMT, FORM, ONTO, COHU, and KLIC form a coherent underfollowed AI/HBM advanced-packaging process-control and test cluster; next pass should verify direct HBM/advanced-packaging revenue, backlog, customer qualifications, and repeat orders.

AMKR should be kept as a reference OSAT capacity node rather than a primary underfollowed alpha candidate unless evidence shows high-utilization, higher-margin AI advanced-packaging capacity commitments.

POWL, MOD, AAON, NVT, and BELFB map to AI physical infrastructure nodes, but current evidence is more hypothesis-heavy than the semiconductor-tool cluster and needs filing-backed validation of data-center mix, backlog, customer wins, and margin durability.
Layer 2B still lacks current market-cap, liquidity, valuation, analyst-coverage, and ownership checks for all tickers; these are required before Layer 2C prioritization.
Need to separate AI-driven demand from cyclical recovery in semicap equipment, OSAT, industrial electrical equipment, HVAC, and electronic components.

For the data-center electrical and cooling candidates, falsification should focus on lack of hyperscaler/colocation exposure, normal industrial-cycle backlog, falling lead times, customer dual-sourcing, and margin normalization.

COHR mapped to AI optical interconnect as an underfollowed photonics supplier; relationship is inferential until filings confirm datacom mix, 800G/1.6T exposure, AI customer concentration, and margin recovery.
LITE mapped to AI optical interconnect as an underfollowed photonics supplier; retained as a hypothesis because telecom-cycle recovery could be confused with AI datacom demand.
VICR mapped to AI-server power delivery as a speculative shadow candidate; survival requires evidence of current AI accelerator design wins and scalable production volumes.

UCTT and ICHR mapped to semicap subsystems one layer below equipment OEMs; the AI relationship is indirect and should be validated against leading-edge logic, memory, and advanced-packaging capex exposure.
AEIS and MKSI mapped to precision power/process-control/photonics subsystems; both need segment-level evidence to separate AI-linked demand from broad semicap or industrial cyclicality.

STRL, IESC, and FIX mapped to data-center construction, electrical balance-of-plant, and cooling/mechanical services; these are underfollowed second-order AI infrastructure relationships needing backlog and customer-mix validation.

LEU mapped to nuclear fuel and power-capacity adjacency as a speculative shadow AI relationship; the link is several steps removed and should not be upgraded without utility, DOE, HALEU, or data-center power procurement evidence.

Company-specific filing-backed evidence is still missing for all tickers in this chunk; current mapping relies on Layer 1 hypotheses, cached theme-level evidence, and supply-chain logic rather than direct verified order/backlog disclosures.

Need a market-pricing check for each ticker: current market cap, EV/sales or EV/EBITDA, analyst coverage, ownership, liquidity, short interest, and whether the AI exposure is already explicitly priced.

Need falsification checks for optical and infrastructure names: hyperscaler capex slowdown, transceiver inventory correction, customer dual-sourcing, telecom recovery misread as AI growth, labor constraints, project margin compression, and grid interconnection delays.

BE should be retained as an underfollowed-lane hypothesis tied to distributed generation for AI data centers, but it requires company-specific contract, margin, fuel, and deployment evidence before it can survive later layers.

VRT and ETN are reference anchors for data-center electrical and thermal balance-of-plant; their main Layer 2B value is benchmarking smaller suppliers in switchgear, UPS, busway, liquid cooling, enclosures, and field services.

CEG and VST are reference anchors for reliable power and power-market exposure; direct AI relevance depends on signed PPAs, regional data-center load, generation constraints, and regulatory approvals.

TSM, NVDA, AVGO, ANET, ASML, and CRWV should be treated primarily as demand or chokepoint reference nodes, not underfollowed candidates, because they are high-attention names that help map lower-level suppliers.

Need fresh filing-backed validation for BE, VRT, ETN, CEG, VST, and CRWV because the provided evidence supports the broad AI power/cooling/grid bottleneck but does not prove each ticker's direct AI revenue, backlog, margin, or contract exposure.

The chunk lacks underfollowed small/mid-cap suppliers beneath VRT, ETN, ANET, AVGO, ASML, and TSM; next funnel pass should deliberately search for obscure suppliers in power distribution, transformer components, liquid cooling, precision optical substrates, probe cards, inspection/metrology, and advanced-packaging inputs.

Market-pricing checks are still missing for all tickers in the chunk, including current market cap, valuation, consensus growth, short interest, analyst coverage, ownership concentration, and whether the AI infrastructure narrative is already discounted.
